extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying evidence and defenses in patent infringement litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Evidentiary and procedural standards for proving title, infringement, and common defenses (noninfringement, nonuse, expired term, license/co-ownership) in patent infringement suits. Focuses on burdens of proof, admissible evidence, presumptions, and the weight to be given to various types of proof (assignments, models, expert testimony, patents, circumstantial evidence, licenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of title/assignment from patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden rests upon him to establish the conveyances by which he claims to have derived his title from the patentee. The original assignment or grant is admissible for this purpose, though not recorded before the action was commenced, and is sufficient if in writing and executed in conformity with the local law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of original instruments, certified copies from the Patent Office may be offered. The defendant may attack existence or validity of the alleged conveyances, or set up a legal title acquired for valuable consideration, without notice, after the three months for recording the plaintiff's conveyance has elapsed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certified Patent Office copies as prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Certified copies from the records of the Patent Office may be offered, and these not only prove the contents of the records, but are also prima facie evidence of the genuineness of their originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A certified copy of an assignment or record may be read in evidence to the jury; a certified copy of a recorded but unacknowledged instrument is sufficient evidence of its execution unless met by opposing testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: When patent date supplies assignment date
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of all other proof as to the date of an assignment, the date of the patent will be taken as the date of the application and also of the assignment, if before patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the date of assignment is uncertain, courts may impute the patent's dates to assignment when no contrary evidence is produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent is not prima facie evidence of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent is not prima facie evidence that the patentee owns the patented invention in relation to infringement; the plaintiff must prove infringement by other evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a patent may be prima facie evidence of novelty/utility for some purposes, it does not relieve the plaintiff of proving that the defendant has made, used, or sold the patented invention in violation of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on plaintiff to prove making/using/selling (infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden rests upon the plaintiff to show by extraneous evidence that the defendant has made, used, or sold the patented invention; if the testimony is of equal weight on either point the defendant must prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plaintiff makes out a prima facie case, the defendant must answer it by evidence (not mere assertion in pleadings); plaintiff may not in rebuttal unexpectedly strengthen his case to the defendant's surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity determined by comparison or inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defendant acts under a separate patent the identity of the inventions is ascertained by comparing the claims of the patents; when the defendant acts without a patent, identity is best shown by actual inspection of the two inventions or of models exhibiting essential attributes, with or without expert explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspection of inventions in actual use is desirable when practicable; designs often manifest identity to a careful observer. If inspection suffices, it is strong evidence; otherwise expert testimony may be used to explain characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony of experts familiar with the defendant's invention may be offered to disclose its characteristics and their agreement or disagreement with those in the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert opinion is not controlling if the question is one of law or patent construction; if the court can say on inspection that the defendant's device does not infringe, there is no room for expert evidence or jury action. The weight of expert opinion depends on circumstances; it cannot override clear inspection-based conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment and refusal to exhibit raises presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant conceals the art or article he uses and declines to produce it for inspection, there is a strong presumption that it is identical with the one covered by the plaintiff's patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The refusal of a defendant to exhibit his device or to permit inspection may be treated by the jury as evidence of infringement; similarly, failure to deny alleged infringing acts when supported by probable testimony may weigh against defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of proof measured against defendant's available evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of proof required from the plaintiff on identity/infringement is measured by the quantity which the defendant can present. The uncontradicted evidence of a single witness that the defendant employed a device substantially like the plaintiff's is sufficient; if contradicted, the jury must find for the defendant unless a clear preponderance supports the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where testimony is evenly balanced, doubts incline the jury in favor of the defendant; a single, uncontradicted witness can be enough to prove infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity focuses on operative principle, not mere form
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute identity or infringement, it is not necessary that the structure or machine used by the defendant should be the same in appearance, form, or proportions as that invented and patented; if the operative principle of the two machines is the same, substantial identity exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple changes in form or proportion do not create a new invention if the operative principle remains the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral or accidental similarity requires conclusive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant's device was intended for the same purpose but the alleged infringement is purely collateral or accidental, the proof of identity must be so conclusive as to leave no other reasonable construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the defendant's device serves a different purpose or was not intended to evade the patent, stronger proof is required to find infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff limited to his patent's claims and descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must abide by the claims and descriptions contained in his own patent, neither adding nor discarding anything to bring his invention into correspondence with that of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff's case cannot be expanded beyond the patent specification and claims to shoehorn the defendant's device into infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant may prove essential differences or superior utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show that notwithstanding resemblances, the means he uses are essentially different; he may offer evidence of substantial superiority of his art or device as the basis of an inference that a distinct idea is expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of different operative means or of superior utility supports a noninfringement finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use or prior patent as defense to identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may prove that the invention he practices is identical with one in use before the date of the plaintiff's inventive act, since if the plaintiff's invention was actually new it cannot be the same as the defendant's earlier use or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of prior use or prior patent may defeat an identity/infringement claim; issues of priority must be proved by adequate evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of defendant's later patent as evidence (good faith / distinctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A later patent obtained by the defendant (or his licensor) may be produced to show (1) the good faith of the defendant and (2) that expert examiners in the Patent Office regarded the invention as essentially distinct from the earlier patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a Patent Office decision is strong evidence for the defendant on identity but does not control the jury; a re-issue or extension increases its weight. If defendant originally secured a patent by disclaiming plaintiff's invention and later re-issued to cover it, defense must rest on priority of inventive act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstantial evidence can establish making/using/selling
rubrics_metrics.description: Because direct testimony is often unobtainable and the facts frequently lie within the defendant's knowledge, the jury may base a finding on circumstantial evidence (possession, factory presence, workmen testimony, advertising, etc.) that tends to prove making, using, or selling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of use or sale combined with evidence that defendant did not procure the articles elsewhere may establish making. Testimony that the device was in defendant's possession or factory, if not denied or explained, can be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisements and sales as evidence of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the defendant advertised the patented articles for sale is admissible as tending to prove actual making, use, or sale, according to other circumstances shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sale to an agent or to others may be evidence of infringement in context; sale to patentee or to agent employed by patentee is not per se infringement but may be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to allow inspection is adverse to defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant's refusal to allow his articles or processes to be inspected, and even his failure to deny the alleged infringing acts when evidenced by probable testimony, are matters which may weigh against him with the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat nonproduction or secrecy as a circumstance supporting inference of infringement; suppression raises presumption against defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency defense requires proof of principal and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant disclaims liability on the ground that he was acting under orders (agency), he must sustain this position by sufficient evidence disclosing the name of the principal and establishing the existence of such authority as renders the principal responsible and excludes the defendant's voluntary choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency defenses must be supported by testimony showing the principal and the scope of authority; mere assertion is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent date and term are prima facie evidence of being in force
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of the patent and the term which it purports to cover appear on the face of the instrument and afford prima facie evidence that the patent was in force during the entire period described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant asserts that the patent had previously expired or been surrendered/repealed, the defendant bears the burden to prove that fact (surrender/repeal or that the term is erroneously stated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlong term in patent limited to lawful period
rubrics_metrics.description: If the term stated in the patent is greater than the seventeen years permitted by the statutes, it is incorrect on its face and the patent will be held valid only for the lawful period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will restrict an overstated term to the statutory maximum; claimant seeking to limit the term bears the burden of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation by prior foreign patent requires production and linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who claims the patent's term should be restricted because of a prior foreign patent must produce the foreign patent covering the invention, or a certified copy from the Patent Office, and establish by sufficient evidence the connection of the plaintiff or his assignor with its prior issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the patentees' names are identical the outside evidence must show identity of persons; when different persons, relations (contracts, correspondence, co-operation, profit participation, etc.) must be shown to connect the foreign patent to the domestic patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof required for co-ownership or express written license
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defendant claims to be a part-owner, assignee, grantee, or express licensee under the patent, his title must be shown by the written instruments of conveyance or a certified copy from the Patent Office; if an express written license exists it must be produced or its absence accounted for and parol evidence of its contents given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An absolute license in the defendant's possession will be presumed delivered until the contrary appears. An oral license may be proved by proper testimony. Slight evidence may be sufficient where the defendant has means to disprove the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license rules (make/use/sell)
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to make may be implied from an express license to use or sell when the latter rights could not be reasonably enjoyed without manufacturing; likewise a license to use or sell may be implied from an express license to make when necessary. A lawful sale without restrictions by one authorized under the patent carries the right to use (and sometimes to sell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license to employ a specific process may arise from sale of a device whose sole utility is in connection with that process. The nature and sources of the defendant's evidence depend on the facts giving rise to the implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiations vs. executed license; conditional licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiations for a license do not prove an actual license; a plea of license must be sustained as a completed contract to end the case. If a license is conditional the defendant must perform the conditions, and if he justifies under the license he must show that its conditions were performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license given as part of a settlement is not evidence against a stranger; a licensee who fails to pay royalties raises questions about whether the license still exists, which is for the court to decide in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior judgment of infringement bears weight
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior judgment finding that a given device infringes a patent is entitled to weight to show that similar devices are also infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior judicial findings are persuasive evidence but do not automatically control later cases involving similar devices; their relevance depends on similarity of devices and issues decided.
